paper_title: Efficient Video Retrieval Augmented Generation via Token Allocation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Efficient long-video understanding requires identifying relevant evidence while minimizing the tokens processed by vision-language models (VLMs). Existing video retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods rely on frame selection and token compression, but overlook how much each additional token is worth. We introduce Lembas, a plug-and-play framework that formulates video RAG as a token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under a shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of a token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in a single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has a provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLM's attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.7-17.3x fewer TFLOPs.

We introduce Lembas, plugand-play framework that formulates video RAG as token allocation problem over frames and subtitles under shared budget. Our key insight is that the value of token diminishes within each item and decreases further as similar evidence receives more tokens. Lembas captures both effects in single objective and solves it with an efficient iterative water-filling algorithm that has provable convergence guarantee. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas reuses the tokens processed in earlier turns and refines relevance with the VLMs attention at no extra cost. Our evaluations show that Lembas improves accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines at comparable compute. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves up to 1.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.717.3 fewer TFLOPs. 1. Introduction Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in video understanding, enabling tasks ranging from action recognition to complex visual question answering [2, 47]. However, extending these capabilities to long videos, such as sports broadcasts, personal recordings, and surveillance footage, remains challenging. Processing every frame can easily exceed the VLMs context window and incur prohibitive inference costs [6, 56]. Efficient longvideo understanding requires identifying and processing the evidence most useful for answering each query. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) addresses this challenge by retrieving relevant frames rather than processing the entire video. Embedding-based RAG retrieves Equal advising contribution. However, these optimizations select relevant evidence items yet often overlook an inherent distinction: different queries require different amounts of evidence and visual detail. For example, identifying small object may require fine-grained information from particular frame, whereas reconstructing an event sequence may benefit from broader temporal coverage. Recent approaches improve this trade-off through adaptive frame selection and token compression. Frame selection methods identify relevant or diverse frames using retrieval heuristics [37, 42, 44, 49, 57, 65], learned policies [5, 27, 58, 59], or agentic search [48, 66]. Token compression methods reduce visual redundancy through token merging or pruning [11, 40, 45]. More recent methods adapt token counts using relevance-proportional allocation [33], discrete resolution tiers [62], or agentic budget planning [1]. Despite these advances, allocation is largely guided by independent relevance scores or predefined rules. Our key insight is that token efficiency requires globally allocating tokens according to their marginal value. We make two observations. First, additional tokens exhibit diminishing returns: once frame preserves sufficient detail, allocating more tokens yields progressively smaller accu1 Reusing evidence across turns. Multi-turn conversations often revisit the same evidence, but different queries may require different token counts, complicating KV-cache reuse. Lembas addresses this through query-independent token ranking, allowing subsequent turns to prefill only tokens missing from the cache. Moreover, we leverage the VLMs attention to cached evidence to refine its relevance for subsequent allocations without additional VLM calls (3.4). We evaluate Lembas on MLVU, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME with Qwen3-VL-8B and InternVL3.5-4B (4). With comparable compute budgets (Fig. 1 and Tab. 1), Lembas improves accuracy by 0.17.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines. On the multi-turn benchmark MT-Video-Bench, Lembas achieves 0.31.5 percentage points higher accuracy than baselines with 1.717.3 fewer TFLOPs. Overall, this paper makes the following contributions: We introduce Lembas, token-efficient video RAG framework that formulates video understanding as token allocation problem under limited budget. We develop Token Allocator that uses iterative waterfilling to efficiently solve the token optimization problem. We extend Lembas to multi-turn conversations through incremental allocation and attention refinement, enabling evidence reuse as allocations change. 2. Related Work Retrieval-augmented generation for video understanding. Video RAG [28] extends retrieval-augmented generation to long videos, whose frames far exceed the context window of VLM. Existing systems differ mainly in how they index video and how they retrieve evidence from this index. For indexing, one line of work converts the video into textual surrogates, such as captions, speech transcripts, and on-screen text, and retrieves over them [32, 34], while another embeds frames or clips directly and retrieves by queryvisual similarity, including across video corpora [23] and live streams [54]. To capture relations that such flat indices miss, structured indices further organize the video into trees [50] or entityand event-centric graphs [38, 41, 55]. For retrieval, single-step similarity search has been extended to multi-step and agentic retrieval, which refines the retrieved evidence over several rounds [41, 55]. However, these systems improve what to index and retrieve, and pass every retrieved item to the VLM at its full, uniform token cost. Lembas instead addresses how many tokens each retrieved item should receive, operating as plug-and-play module downstream of these retrievers. Keyframe or token selection. Rather than fully processing long videos to answer user questions, various methods intelligently decide which frames to process [29, 30, 37, 42 Figure 2. Varying the tokens per frame allows Lembas to retain evidence from more frames within shared budget. racy gains. Second, token value depends on other allocated evidence: frame contributes less new information when similar frames already receive tokens. Naturally, one fundamental problem is to distribute shared token budget across frames and subtitles to maximize their aggregate utility. Building on these observations, we introduce Lembas, plug-and-play framework for token-efficient video RAG  (Fig. 3)  . Given frames and subtitles retrieved by an existing RAG system, Lembas captures their utility, allocates shared token budget, and prunes each item accordingly before VLM inference. Realizing this design faces two challenges: modeling token value and optimizing allocations efficiently. Moreover, users rarely ask single question about video, and conversation that spans multiple turns raises third challenge: reusing evidence as allocations change across turns. Modeling token value. An items contribution depends not only on its relevance to the query, but also on how many tokens it receives and how much of its content is already covered by other items. We characterize downstream accuracy across token counts and find that concave, saturating rational function well captures diminishing returns  (Fig. 4)  . We combine this modeling with query relevance and redundancy awareness, and use attention-based pruning to realize the resulting token counts (3.2). Solving token allocation. Accounting for redundancy makes token allocations interdependent, exploding the combination space. We develop iterative water-filling, which repeatedly updates diversity-aware relevance and solves closed-form water-filling subproblem. Our solver converges to the global optimum of the continuous relaxation with an O(1/ℓ) objective gap after ℓ iterations (3.3). 44, 49, 59, 65], either due to practical constraints (e.g., the context window [61]) or to improve efficiency via reduced token prefill costs [6, 56]. Token pruning has been widely studied in long-context LLM serving. H2O [63] prunes tokens with smaller accumulated attention, while StreamingLLM [52] retains the initial and recent tokens. Beyond which frames or tokens to keep, recent and concurrent works decide how much to spend on each frame, typically by routing frames to few fixed resolution tiers through agentic search [1] or hand-crafted rules [33, 62]. Lembas instead treats this question as resource allocation problem, formulating an objective, solving it with convergence guarantee, and extending it to multi-turn conversations. Conventional resource allocation. Resource allocation has been widely studied in networked and computing systems to distribute limited resources among competing demands [13, 26, 31]. Classical approaches include utility maximization and pricing mechanisms [7, 35], water-filling and power control [14, 39, 60], and fairness-aware scheduling [16, 18, 21]. Lembas brings this resource allocation perspective to video understanding, allocating finite token resource across retrieved items via iterative water-filling. 3. Method Lembas is plug-and-play framework that makes video RAG token-efficient. As shown in Fig. 3, given query, Lembas scores the relevance of each frame and subtitle, optimizes their allocation under token budget, and retains the highest-ranked tokens from each selected item. Its Token Allocator exploits diminishing returns in token value and discounts redundant evidence. For multi-turn conversations, Lembas further reuses tokens already in the KV cache and refines their relevance using the VLMs attention. 3.1. Problem Formulation Consider video and query q. Prior methods allocate tokens by fixed rules rather than by optimizing an objective. QuoTA [33] assigns each frame token count proportional to its relevance, while Q-Frame [62] assigns the same token count to all frames within relevance tier. On Video-MME, removing subtitle allocation decreases overall accuracy by 3.6 points, with particularly large 7.3-point drop on long videos. Even without subtitle allocation, Lembas outperforms all similarly budgeted, non-agentic frame selection baselines by 0.63.6 points. Removing the diversity term reduces accuracy by 0.7 points, confirming the benefit of modeling redundancy, and replacing water-filling with simpler proportional allocation, which offers no optimality guarantee, reduces it by 1.2 points. For multi-turn conversations, removing attention refinement decreases accuracy by 1.1 points while increasing prefill compute from 275 to 315 TFLOPs. Disabling incremental allocation increases compute from 275 to 687 TFLOPs (2.5), with only 0.6-point accuracy increase. These results show that attention refinement improves evidence selection, while incremental allocation is the primary driver of multi-turn compute savings. 5. Conclusion We introduce Lembas, plug-and-play framework for token-efficient video RAG that jointly allocates shared token budget across frames and subtitles. Its Token Allocator optimizes query relevance, diminishing token value, and evidence diversity through iterative water-filling, while incremental allocation and attention refinement enable efficient reuse across conversational turns. At comparable compute, Lembas improves accuracy by 0.17.2 percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines. On multi-turn video understanding, Lembas achieves 0.31.5 percentage points higher accuracy with 1.717.3 fewer TFLOPs. Figure 8. Main Results Lembas achieves the Pareto frontier across single-turn video understanding. As shown in Tab. 1, Lembas achieves the highest overall accuracy across all three benchmarks and both VLM backbones. With Qwen3-VL-8B, it improves over Top-K by 2.2, 2.6, and 4.2 percentage points on MLVU, LVB, and Video-MME, respectively, at comparable compute. The gains are particularly pronounced on long videos: on the long subset of Video-MME, Lembas improves accuracy from 63.6% to 71.7% with nearly identical TFLOPs. QuoTA achieves competitive accuracy but incurs 2.83.4 higher compute due to its VLM-based frame scoring. These trends generalize to InternVL3.5-4B, where Lembas improves over Top-K by 0.53.5 points. Furthermore, Lembas consistently achieves favorable accuracy compute trade-offs across multiple token budgets (Fig. 8a). When integrated with VideoRAG, Lembas improves accuracy by 0.4 and 2.2 percentage points on MLVU and Video-MME, respectively, by allocating tokens across more frames at comparable compute, while accuracy decreases by 0.7 points on LVB. These results demonstrate that Lembas complements existing RAG designs. Lembas achieves the Pareto frontier across multi-turn video understanding. As shown in Fig. 8b, Lembas outperforms all baselines by 0.31.5 percentage points while requiring 1.717.3 fewer TFLOPs. Unlike prior methods that reuse only previously selected frames or exact resolution matches, Lembas incrementally prefills only tokens not already present in the KV cache. This finer-grained reuse substantially reduces redundant computation across conversational turns while preserving answer accuracy. Lembas introduces negligible compute overhead. sections.content: We were assisted by various LLMs, specifically from the ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini model families in preparing this work. They were used to assist in paper writing, related work search, and coding which the authors reviewed and edited. LLMs were used to lesser extent in the design and analysis of core ideas and experiments. Gemini 3.8 Flash was used to evaluate multi-turn benchmark results. LLMs were not used to create or annotate data. The authors take full responsibility for all content.
